Auracast broadcasts are an integral part of the storytelling in this off-Broadway show about love, connections, and hearing loss.
Up a few concrete steps and through the front door of a 200-year-old row house in New York City, I follow a crowd of people into the 178-seat SoHo Playhouse. As we filter to our seats, ushers hand each person a black drawstring bag with a pair of wired headphones connected to a small Auracast receiver . Then, soon after the play begins, we’re instructed to put them on.
The headphones are an integral storytelling tool of Love Me — a one-man show from the minds of stand-up comedian and former Saturday Night Live writer Drew Michael and director Prashanth Venkataramanujam. It’s a show about love and the bid for connection, told in five chapters about different relationships in Michael’s life, bound by the threads of his hearing loss and self-discovery.
Love Me ’s experimental sound design is possible thanks to Auracast, a technology based on Bluetooth that can broadcast a high-quality audio stream to any number of nearby devices. As the show follows Michael from childhood through adulthood, sound designer Daniel Kluger uses the headphones in combination with the theater speakers to create experiences that wouldn’t be possible with a traditional setup. Tinnitus ringing and hearing test tones play in the music between sections as subtle clues as the show builds to Michael’s epiphany about his hearing loss. Kluger also explores the world through varying levels of sonic clarity. Sound playing through the theater’s speakers is sometimes intentionally muffled, which is then further dulled by the headphones, giving the audience a sense of what Michael is hearing in those moments.
But one sound that stays clear and pristine is Michael’s inner monologue, heard in the headphones throughout the show. The inner monologue consists of both prerecorded tracks and the live feed from Michael’s microphone on stage as he talks back and forth with himself. “Any time you’re in my head — anything in the headphones is coming through clearly,” Michael tells me after the show. “[We’re] trying to also highlight that the appeal of the inner world is such that it’s the highest fidelity space for this person. It’s more comfortable.”
The different sound sources and treatments of the sound can lead to intentionally confusing scenes for the audience. During one, where Michael is doing a stand-up set at a comedy club, three sounds compete for attention: The theater speakers play the crowd’s reactions (including a heckler whose voice is sometimes muffled and sometimes clear); his prerecorded inner monologue reacting to the crowd plays in the headphones; and on stage, Michael is performing the set, with his mic muffled so our focus is on his inner monologue. It’s one of the definitive moments where the audience feels the constant concentration necessary to parse what’s happening when sounds aren’t clear and become overwhelming.
But the biggest impact comes during a climactic scene the sound design has been building toward, a realization that also incorporates the visuals of a series of Michael’s audiograms over the years. “I had this massive breakthrough about the whole history of what I’ve been doing — the cognitive labor, the invisible to myself labor that was affecting every single minute of my life,” Michael says. “That was a huge moment.”
That’s when the audience is instructed to remove the headphones we’ve been wearing for nearly the entire show. As Michael comes to the recognition of his relationship with his hearing loss and the clarity of mind that gives him, what we’ve become used to for the entire show’s experience — the headphones — are now gone, as is that literal weight from our heads. It’s an emotional moment, one that I’ve thought about multiple times since seeing the show.
It also leads into the final act, where Michael begins to understand his own Deaf identity. “The deafness is not the culprit, it’s the denial of it.” he tells me. “My hearing currently has never been worse, but I’ve never been more self-affirmed or self-actualized or felt happier in myself. It’s a misconception, I think, about deafness as a tragedy, deafness as a deficit, deafness as a burden, deafness as something that plagues a person.”
The ability of Auracast to broadcast an audio stream that any number of headphones can connect to is what made Love Me a possibility. Any Auracast headphones can connect to the audience broadcast — I brought along the Nothing Pro 1 to test the ability and connected to the audience broadcast channel in seconds — but I used the provided Auri receiver and Austrian Audio headset for the performance. The show’s sound was designed with those in mind, and I didn’t want the differing isolation of the Nothing headphones to affect the intent of the experience.
Love Me is presented in partnership with Deaf West Theatre , which supports Deaf-centered storytelling in theatrical productions. In addition to the audience Auracast feed, there’s one for users of hearing aids and cochlear implants that’s designed for compliance with those devices, and iPads with captions are also available. During the performance, Michael connects to his own broadcast channel with Auracast-enabled Phonak Eon Sphere hearing aids. “We talked about using in-ear monitors, but if I use an in-ear monitor, then I don’t have amplification from my environment, so then I lose contact with the audience,” Michael says. “These function as two things: They’re hearing aids and also in-ear monitors.”
Love Me relies on the Auracast technology to tell its story, but it isn’t a story about hearing technology. The technology is there to tell the story of connection and discovery of identity. “I think right now … there are two things that are at odds — the hearing aid and audiological tech side of deafness and then the cultural identity side of deafness,” Michael says. Technological improvements, like cochlear implants and hearing aids, are cited as one of the reasons schools for the deaf have been on the decline, which leads to kids being mainstreamed (put into regular public schools) and losing out on Deaf history and culture. “I’m not against the tech,” Michael says, “I just think tech and Deaf identity should be a marriage rather than a divide.”
And that collaboration is why Love Me works as well as it does. The Auracast technology is there both for accessibility — in the same way it’s already used in other performances, lectures, or announcement systems — and to uplift the show’s story of love, acceptance, and acknowledgement of one’s own Deaf identity. It’s an inventive use of the technology that carries with it a powerful message.

After I published my review of the HomeView , Apple’s first smart display , y’all still had a ton of questions about how it works as a smart speaker . So, I spent a bunch more time testing its audio capabilities and support for third-party music apps — and found a few more frustrations along the way. Here are the answers to all your burning questions. Have more? I’ll answer them in the comments.
The HomeView isn’t a replacement for a Sonos One, a full-size HomePod, or a similar-size speaker. Those are much better speakers. In size and sound, the HomeView is closer to the HomePod Mini. I tested it alongside the Mini 2 (which sounds marginally better than the first-gen Mini) and found the tabletop HomeView mostly comparable, with these caveats: The HomeView has better bass and is slightly louder, but it’s not as clear and is less room-filling.
You can hear them both in action in this video, alongside the full-size HomePod, the Sonos One, and the wall-mounted HomeView:
The difference comes down to the hardware. The Mini 2 has a single full-range driver and two passive radiators, whereas the tabletop HomeView has two drivers in the display, plus a woofer and two passive radiators in its base. While the woofer adds some oomph, the HomeView’s display, which sits over the speaker base, partly covers it, affecting the sound compared to the Mini. Apple added an accelerometer to the display because tilting it changes the sound, so HomeView adjusts its EQ in real time based on the angle. Still, the Mini, while not as loud, fills a room better, thanks partly to its 360-degree sound. (The HomeView supports Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, which the Mini 2 doesn’t.)
The wall-mounted HomeView has only two drivers, with computational audio Apple says is “tuned specifically for on-wall placement.” It sounds fine but is noticeably thinner than the tabletop version, and bass is basically non-existent. I wouldn’t recommend it for its sound quality, but it’s great for talking to a visitor through your video doorbell .
No. While you can group HomeViews with any other AirPlay speakers to play music out of them all at once, you can’t pair two for a stereo setup or pair a HomeView with a HomePod or Mini. I like the sound of two Minis paired in stereo and use this setup in my office and my bedroom. They also work as speakers for my Apple TVs in those rooms.
If you have $300 to spend on a good-sounding smart speaker setup, go with two Minis over a HomeView. The HomeView’s real benefit is the screen. I cover its uses extensively in my full review , but for audio in particular, I like that the screen acts like a jukebox, making it easy to change songs, select new music, and scroll through your podcasts or audiobooks — without needing to find a quarter! With a HomePod, you rely on Siri voice control or your Apple device to select content.
You can AirPlay to the HomeView as with any other AirPlay speaker, and audio handoff works the same as it does on HomePods. Tap your phone to the HomeView, and whatever is playing transfers to the speakers and the screen. Handoff also works in reverse, letting you send any content back to your phone. One addition with the HomeView: You can now hand off video.
In testing, handoff worked for Apple TV, Apple Music, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Pocket Casts, YouTube Music, FaceTime, and phone calls — although phone calls sometimes dropped. YouTube and YouTube TV videos also handed off, even though they don’t have an app on the HomeView. But Netflix and Amazon Prime Video only played audio, though both played video in the Safari browser .
One word of caution: Handoff is aggressive. As with HomePods, if you’re holding your phone within a few inches, the HomeView will try to hand off content.
HomeView doesn’t let you set a default speaker or group to use instead of its built-in speaker. However, you can play audio to any AirPlay speaker or group of speakers. I tested this on HomePods, Sonos speakers, and a Samsung TV, and it worked smoothly.
For native apps (Apple Music, Podcasts, and Safari), the HomeView remembers the last speaker or speaker pair you used and automatically plays content through those when you return. If it’s been a while since you opened the app, it pops up the option to choose the last-used speakers.
Spotify has no search box because you’re not supposed to type while driving — only I’m not driving; I’m in my kitchen!
Things get messier with third-party audio apps such as Spotify and Audible, and with Apple apps that use the CarPlay interface, such as Apple News and Apple TV. The HomeView only automatically uses the last speakers if you choose content from the HomeView screen. If you use Siri voice control, it defaults to the HomeView speaker.
So, “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan from Spotify” played music from HomeView’s speaker and not the stereo pair of Minis in my office, where I’d last been listening to Spotify. I could direct it to play music there by adding “on Office,” but that’s more of a mouthful than just “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan,” which is all you need to say if you use Apple Music.
Which brings me to another one of your most-asked questions — and my biggest complaint about this device as a smart speaker: How does it support third-party audio apps? Like second-class citizens.
Spotify works on the HomeView, but with limitations that apply to all non-native and third-party apps: they only show up when your phone is connected to the HomeView via your profile , so only you can use them.
Apple has taken a shortcut here: Rather than building a dedicated HomeView experience for app developers, the HomeView uses Apple’s existing CarPlay platform . This makes it easier for developers to put their apps on the HomeView — if an audio or video app supports CarPlay, it already works on the HomeView (there’s no support for other types of CarPlay apps).
In practice, this creates frustrating limitations, including no search function and the need for a user profile on the HomeView and your phone on the same Wi-Fi. It also results in slower performance and a laggy, inconsistent experience compared to the native apps.
I tried several apps: Pocket Casts, Amazon Music, YouTube Music, Spotify, and Audible. They all appeared in my HomeView app drawer, and I could access them, choose content via streamlined interfaces, and then play audio on the HomeView or AirPlay from it to any speakers.
But CarPlay apps don’t work as well as the built-in audio apps — Music, Podcasts, and Safari. They take longer to load and respond more slowly. You also can’t type a search query in any of them, as you can in the native apps, because they don’t have a search field or keyboard. Instead, you have to scroll through content to find what you want or use Siri voice search.
Me: “Siri, resume my Audible book.” Siri: “Shuffling latest songs from Apple Music.”
There’s no search box because you’re not supposed to type while driving; only I’m not driving — I’m in my kitchen! Large language models can now redesign your TV and upgrade your camera for you. Is the physical world ready to be Claude Code-d?
This is The Stepback , a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce . The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here .
Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of.
For one developer in India who goes by Gathin T, the whole thing started almost on a whim. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. His was a set made by Xiaomi and running Android TV, with so many ads and so much interface chaos it was hard to even change inputs. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?”
Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He posted on X about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the most popular repositories on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen.
Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to share the process so widely.) But for vibe hackers everywhere, the good news is that Android kind of runs everything. From dishwashers to digital photo frames to luxury cars, even gadgets that don’t look like Android often run Android. Even when they don’t, odds are good that there’s another way in. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking.
Again, few of the technical capabilities here are new, and enterprising developers have been doing this kind of work for many years. Some have even been using AI for several years to make the work easier. But when Claude Code first had its “oh my gosh it works” moment in late 2025, developers began leaning on the tools even more — and non-developers began discovering they, too, could build software now. And over the course of 2026, more and more people began pointing that capability at their hardware.
Now, it seems, all hardware is hacker hardware. Camera enthusiasts embraced the possibilities of vibe hacking as fast as anyone, using LLMs to repackage their camera software in all sorts of ways. Firmware hacks like Magic Lantern are a staple of the camera community, but suddenly it seems like everyone is using AI to add new recording capabilities, support higher resolutions, or even add new looks and color profiles to their shots. Many are using the tools to give their old gear new life; other, more enterprising vibe coders are pointing their bots at their brand-new hardware.
The music world is being similarly upended . Budding musicians are turning cheap synths into powerful new kinds of gear, and a cheap gadget known as the M-Vave FM-1 has become a popular target for custom firmware and new features. M-Vave has even released an open-source firmware, embracing the hackers as other companies have tried to keep them out. The FM-1 is cheap, it’s easy to hack, and it’s raising questions about what higher-end manufacturers can even do to compete.
Gamers, who are also using AI to decompile and mod the games they love, are using LLMs to add new features to their consoles. One vibe coder found a way to play PlayStation 2 discs on a PlayStation 5; lots of gamers have built scripts that allow them to use their favorite controllers on other devices.
In the games world in particular, this has caused the industry to fight back. Game makers are looking for ways to protect their work from being decompiled and made available for free and on other platforms. Luke Dicken, a longtime gaming executive who was recently Take-Two’s head of artificial intelligence, recently predicted to Kotaku that the industry will start to embrace “more invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and probably more of a push towards streaming solutions since nobody can decompile what they can’t get their hands on.” Hardware makers will push harder to lock down their systems; companies across the board will pursue legal action to protect their intellectual property.
All this hardware access also creates new risks for users. When you install a vibe-coded version of your camera’s firmware, you are now well outside the bounds of what the camera manufacturer is equipped to help you solve. You might be stuck asking Claude to fix the problems Claude created. As Ritchie Roesch wrote recently at Fuji X Weekly , “It’s not so much if someone’s camera will become a permanent paperweight, it’s a matter of when and how many, and whether it will be yours.”
The safer (and less litigious ) route for the enterprising vibe hacker lies in an entirely new kind of hardware. ESP32 modules, which package networking chips, microphones, speakers, and more into a simple and hacker-friendly package, are suddenly everywhere in hardware communities. (Think Raspberry Pis, but even cheaper and more versatile.) So sure, you can use Claude Code to jailbreak and de-Amazon your Kindle , but why do that when you can buy a device like the M5Stack PaperMono, an ESP32-based e-paper device you can make into whatever you want?
ESP32 modules are perfectly suited to help you build the kind of hyper-specific device Apple or Samsung would never consider. With a few dollars and a few prompts, you can build a way to see real-time sea conditions , rig up a monitor for your whole DJ system , or just play Metal Gear Solid on the go. You can even have a dedicated device for your family’s shopping list.
The arms race between device manufacturers and vibe hackers is only going to continue. As AI models get more powerful, and both the tools and their users get more sophisticated, it’ll be easier and easier for anyone to point their bot at their TV, their car, or their washing machine and see what happens. Some manufacturers will try their best to keep the hackers out; others will look for ways to safely embrace them. Some users will find incredible new functionality for their tech; others will find they’ve created extraordinarily large and expensive paperweights.
Before long, we’re going to see a lot of ESP32 devices turned into more consumer-friendly hardware. Meta is already leading the charge with its Muse Charm and the Muse Gadgets program, through which you can either buy a nicely packaged ESP32 module or use your own to quickly spin up a dedicated AI device. This kind of gadget — just a simple computing module in a pretty box — is going to be everywhere.

All these tech outages are a reminder we’re at the mercy of powers beyond our comprehension. At least in GTA we have control
T his week marked the release of the highly anticipated video game Grand Theft Auto VI . Millions around the world checked out of their usual responsibilities in order to immerse themselves in a game where you run errands for your girlfriend in between murdering people.
I feel completely alone in not caring about GTA VI, as I famously only play video games where you get to be RoboCop – issuing public nuisance citations to graffiti taggers in between murdering people. I’m a man who knows what he likes.
GTA VI has been over a decade in the making. The anticipation built to a fever pitch, with gaming enthusiasts practically going feral at the prospect of finally getting to schlep groceries and engage in casual bird-watching after brutally running over a pedestrian with a stolen Porsche.
Our collective addiction to virtual mayhem is guaranteed to crash productivity all across the globe. I shudder to think what would happen if the game glitched out for everyone all at once, rendering your PS5 a slickly manufactured plastic paperweight. Would there be Paris-style riots turning every major city into a dystopian nightmare riddled with flaming trash bins and smashed shop windows?
In a sense, that would be a boon to fans of the game, as the world of flesh would start to resemble GTA come to blood-curdling life.
Meanwhile, gaming is trending in the opposite direction. Most modern video game systems don’t even accept physical media anymore. The days of buying an actual disc in a little plastic box are nearly gone. Each game purchase is now just exchanging invisible digital money for the right to access the pixels and data that make virtual worlds come to life on your TV screen. It’s ephemeral, intangible, and it could all disappear in an instant.
But hey, that’s life in 2026, a time when hackers can turn off your refrigerator from halfway around the world. GTA VI digitally vaporizing at random would be catastrophic, but it wouldn’t be the first computer-related global inconvenience of the year, let alone the month or the week.
For the last seven days, the news has been dominated by outages in our tech infrastructure : grounded planes, broken email systems, bank accounts fritzing in and out of existence like a flickering lightbulb. The troubles have been blamed on software bugs, faulty patches, and outdated equipment.
The truly bored among us prefer to claim worldwide conspiracy theories, malicious hackers, or government manipulation that would have James Bond tossing his martini in the air and screaming: “This is all too much for me to handle.”
Meanwhile, AI companies like Anthropic are growing exponentially as they seek to further entangle everyday life on Earth with their complex, interdependent, free-thinking computer systems.
Even if these outages aren’t the direct result of AI, it’s all part of our brave new world. For the simple price of your money occasionally being completely inaccessible, you can have AI write a novel for you or remind you to pay your car insurance bill with the money you can’t use.
This plan seems to be a huge success for everyone but actual human beings with normal, non-billionaire lives. Besides tech companies, I suppose the other biggest winners in all this are bar owners, especially the ones at airports. When absolutely nothing works, the only sane response is to have a pint and laugh about it.
Increasingly, reality resembles a video game like GTA VI. Maybe without all the gruesome, wanton mayhem and surface-to-air missiles, but certainly with all of the other bits. As games start folding in more mundane tasks like shopping, going to the gym, or fixing a leaky roof, real life is taking on the rigid, mission-based thrill ride of the arcade.
Sorting through a health insurance claim is almost as annoying as a boss fight in a classic Sonic the Hedgehog game – repeated button-smashing, gnashed teeth, and frayed nerves. The mere notion of a shadowy cabal flipping switches to shut off various critical services makes me think of a caffeine-addled bachelor cackling as they wreak havoc in a particularly malicious game of Sim City.
I often feel like a cuckolded non-playable game character, or NPC, watching more exciting events happen around me that I’m unable to control. If I want to be able to get on an airplane that actually leaves on time, I’m going to have to level up my XP or purchase a pay-to-win upgrade.
It’s not uncommon for me to imagine myself as an NPC avatar while strapped into the back of a Waymo driverless taxi, tooling from one checkpoint to another, silently praying the computer shuttling me to my destination doesn’t decide to change its mind and fly off a bridge into a river.
We’re all at the mercy of virtual powers beyond our comprehension. One can’t help but sink into the despairing realization that life is now a series of slights perpetuated by an algorithm with a callous disregard for the whims of corporeal beings.
So, what do we do when nothing works and everything is impossible? Go outside and do some actual bird watching? Repair a real roof instead of one in a video game?
Surely not. If anything, these technological disruptions further underline our need for our gadgets and gizmos to exist. Absence, as they say, makes the heart grow fonder. When Microsoft Outlook crashes, it just reminds people how much they need Microsoft Outlook.
Our dependency on these tools has become second nature, so ingrained in the hum of the world that every so often, they have to go away for us to even notice them. When you can’t access your Chase bank account for a few hours, why wouldn’t you fall to your knees to give thanks to the benevolent tech lord for seeing fit to bring it back to life?
Better, then, to stop worrying about things you can’t control and focus on what you can … in GTA VI. The last vestige of absolute power is inside video games, a realm where you can do everything and anything you want, down to even the most antisocial behavior the mind can conjure.
The main characters of video games have all the agency real people lack. If they run out of money, they can steal a car and get away with it. If all flights are grounded at the airport, they can hijack a helicopter.
The only sane response to the feeling of ineffectual reality is to further retreat into the digital frontier, where anything is possible. After all, there’s only around a month left before Christmas, and your fake digital girlfriend is expecting a gift.

Last year, I nearly quit mathematics. On 20 November, Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The Lean and Mathlib communities have since certified the formal proof. We are only beginning to understand the argument. What kind of future awaits someone beginning a life in mathematics?
In May 2025, I led the number theory team for Epoch AI’s FrontierMath project. We wrote difficult problems to test large language models. I watched an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all the moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves, drawing on work by Manjul Bhargava and Roger Heath-Brown, and on papers my father wrote in the 1960s. I was stunned.
I earned my PhD in 1993 and built a life around research, teaching, and mentoring. I’d love to prove that Ramanujan’s tau function never vanishes, or that half of the partition numbers are even. My 25-year-old self would have been crushed by what we are witnessing today. Nothing I write can reassure someone just starting a career. I can explain why I stayed.
My father, a number theorist, died in January. As a boy, I learned from him about Ramanujan, whose notebooks have occupied mathematicians for generations. Ramanujan believed a Hindu goddess gave him mathematical formulas in his dreams. When I considered working on AI, I feared my father would see it as abandoning mathematics. Instead, he told me AI reminded him of Ramanujan: discoveries from an unexpected source might leave us much to understand. I do not take that comparison literally. Ramanujan was a human with an extraordinary imagination and life. My father’s response brought me to tears. It gave me permission to keep being a mathematician in a way I had not anticipated.
Today, I am on leave from the University of Virginia and work as Founding Mathematician at Axiom Math. We use AI to formalize, verify and extend mathematical proofs in Lean, a language in which a small checking program verifies each step. This work can expose gaps and make proofs inspectable and reusable. Human judgment remains essential: we must check that the formal statement says what we intended.
We released the first complete Lean formalization of the classification of finite simple groups, one of mathematics’ largest proofs. Announced in 1983, the classification required decades of work by many mathematicians; a major gap was filled in 2004. Our AI helped produce 43.1 million lines of Lean code. In the process, we found a problem in a published route to a key theorem and supplied an alternative argument. Lean’s kernel checks the resulting formal proof. The mathematics belongs to the generations who developed it. Our formalizations of the classification and other bodies of math are already helping us build and check further mathematics.
After 24 days of work, I watched the final milestones land on my laptop. I cried. I thought about the people who had made the classification possible, and about the father I could no longer tell. But I am 58. I’ve advised 35 PhD students, 17 postdocs, and hundreds of undergraduates. I’ve had opportunities young mathematicians cannot assume. I cannot ask a graduate student to regard uncertainty as an adventure because I have found rewarding work within it.
At a Berkeley colloquium two days after OpenAI announced its Navier–Stokes solution, a scheduled lecture became a town hall lasting almost two and a half hours. Students asked about credit, transparency, hiring, and how mathematicians whose work came first were treated. Some asked me what I would do to help them. Campus security was locking the building as we left.
The declaration A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics, signed by Terry Tao and other Fields Medalists, warns about rushed announcements, inadequate attribution and the loss of mathematical understanding. I share those concerns. At a National Academies meeting, I put my position this way: hope is not a plan, and nostalgia is not mentoring.
Universities, journals, employers and funding agencies must decide what they support and reward. Students and younger colleagues should have a voice while those decisions are still open, as should mathematicians who choose to work without AI. In the discussions where I have a voice, I will argue for that participation.
Students need room to struggle with mathematics and learn to question the tools they use. In my advising, I will ask what a young mathematician understood, originated, or made possible. Access to a powerful system is no substitute for those contributions. For work I help publish, readers should know what has been proved, what remains assumed, and who contributed the ideas.
I want my students, and their students, to develop ideas that are genuinely their own. I want them to have colleagues who listen and the material support to pursue a mathematical life. My work at Axiom is one part of how I am trying to contribute. It does not replace my obligations as a teacher and mentor. I may be wrong about how this will unfold. I am still learning what it means to be a mathematician.
Ken Ono is a number theorist and professor of mathematics at the University of Virginia, currently on leave as founding mathematician at Axiom Math. A former vice-president of the American Mathematical Society, he is known for his work on Ramanujan and integer partitions.
These views do not necessarily reflect those of Axiom Math, the University of Virginia, the National Academies, or any other institution with which I am affiliated.

ChatGPT ve benzeri yapay zeka uygulamaları öğrenciler arasında yaygınlaşıyor. Araştırmalar, yapay zekanın bilinçsiz kullanımının okul başarısını ve temel becerileri olumsuz etkileyebileceğini gösteriyor.
Yapay zeka uygulamaları öğrenciler arasında giderek yaygınlaşıyor. 15 yaşındaki 9'uncu sınıf öğrencisi Jakob, kendisinin ve arkadaşlarının yaklaşık iki buçuk yıldır yapay zekayı kullandığını anlatıyor. DW'ye konuşan ve gerçek adını söylemek istemeyen Jakob, "Bugün Fransızca sınavım vardı ve dün ChatGPT'den birçok konuyu yeniden açıklamasını istedim. Sınıfımdakilerin çoğu, ev ödevlerini yaptırmak için yapay zeka kullanıyor" diyor.
Matematik, Almanca, İngilizce, kimya veya fizik fark etmiyor, tek bir tıklama ile çözüm veya çözüm yolu ekrana geliyor. Bilim dünyasında bu "düşünme sürecinin başka araçlara aktarılması" olarak tanımlanıyor. Bu durumda düşünme eylemi başka bir araca devrediliyor, bu bir hesap makinesi, bir not kağıdı ya da ChatGPT gibi bir sohbet robotu olabiliyor.
Ancak beyin açısından sorun, problemin tamamının yapay zeka tarafından çözülmesiyle başlıyor. Bir not kağıdı veya hesap makinesi çözüm sürecindeki bazı adımları üstlense de genellikle tüm düşünme sürecini devralmaz. Yapay zeka sohbet robotları ise bunun çok ötesine geçiyor.
Bazen ev ödevlerini yapay zekaya yaptırdığını söyleyen Jakob, ancak "sadece gerçekten çıkmaza girdiği" durumlarda yapay zekaya başvurduğunu anlatıyor. Bunun bir sorun olabileceğinin farkında olan Jakob, "Notları iyi olanlar, bunu pek yapmıyor" diyor.
Yıllardır Almanca öğretmenliği yapan Franziska Müller, bir lisede çalışıyor. DW'ye konuşan Müller, bazı öğrencileri için "Artık kendi başlarına düşünemiyorlar" şeklindeki gözlemini aktarıyor. Adını değiştirdiğimiz Müller, bazı öğrencilerin derste soruları yapay zekaya yazdığını, sıra gelince de fark ettirmeden yapay zekanın verdiği yanıtları okuduklarını anlatıyor.
Öğrencilerin geçmişe kıyasla metinleri kavramakta daha çok zorlandığını söyleyen Müller, "Çünkü daha az okuyorlar ve neredeyse her şeyi yapay zekaya özetletiyorlar" diyor.
Eylül ayında açıklanan PISA araştırması gibi, birçok çalışma benzer sonuçları ortaya koyuyor. Ekonomik İşbirliği ve Kalkınma Örgütü'nün (OECD) yaptırdığı PISA araştırmasını yürütenler, "Belirli ödevlerde yapay zeka sohbet robotlarını kullanan öğrenciler, fen bilimlerinde yapay zekayı kullanmayan öğrencilere kıyasla daha düşük puanlar alıyor" sonucuna vardı.
90'dan fazla ülkeden öğrencilerin katıldığı araştırma, 15 yaş grubuna yönelik dünyanın en kapsamlı uluslararası karşılaştırma çalışması olarak kabul ediliyor. Almanya'daki öğrenciler bu yıl araştırmada şimdiye kadarki en kötü sonuçlardan birini aldı.
PISA'nın yapay zekaya ilişkin bulguları ise oldukça basit: "Nasıl yalnızca spor izleyerek değil, spor yaparak formda kalabiliyorsak; öğrenme de sadece içerik tüketerek değil, bilgi üzerinde düşünerek ve zihinsel çaba harcayarak gerçekleşiyor." Başka bir deyişle, beyinlerini yeterince çalıştırmayanlar, düşünme becerilerini köreltme riskiyle karşı karşıya kalabilir.
ABD merkezli düşünce kuruluşu Brookings Institution eğitim alanında yapay zekânın risklerinin faydalarından daha ağır bastığını savunuyor. Dünyanın farklı ülkelerinden gençlerin katıldığı araştırmada, "temel becerilerin kaybı" ile "eleştirel düşünme, hafıza, odaklanma ve muhakeme yeteneğinin zayıflaması" risklerine dikkat çekiliyor.
Peki, ChatGPT, Claude, Grok veya Meta AI gibi yapay zeka sohbet robotlarının eğitimde giderek artan etkisi karşısında ne yapılmalı?
New York'un sol görüşlü belediye başkanı Zohran Mamdani, 2026-2027 eğitim öğretim yılında devlet okullarında 8'inci sınıfa kadar, yani 14-15 yaşına dek yapay zeka kullanımını yasakladı.
Yasak bir çözüm olabilir mi? Almanya'da ortaöğretim veren bir okulda 10'uncu ve 13'üncü sınıflara Almanca dersi veren Julian Hinn yasağın çözüm olmadığı görüşünde. Herkesin cep telefonu üzerinden yapay zekaya erişebildiğini belirten Hinn, "Bunu evde kullanmayacaklarını düşünenler, gerçekleri görmezden geliyor" diyor.
Almanya'da gençlerin medya kullanımına ilişkin JIM araştırması da bu görüşü destekliyor. Almanya'da bu araştırmaya katılan 12-19 yaş arasındaki gençlerin yüzde 91'i en az bir yapay zeka uygulamasını kullandığını ifade etti. Yüzde 74'ü de yapay zekayı ev ödevlerini yaparken ve ders çalışırken kullandığını belirtti. Bu veriler 2024 yılına ait. Günümüzde bu oranın artmış olabileceği tahmin ediliyor. Brookings Institute'un Asya, Latin Amerika ve ABD'de yaptığı araştırma da gençler arasında yapay zeka kullanımının benzer seviyelerde olduğunu gösteriyor.
Alman siyasetçiler de sorunun farkında. Almanya'da eğitim eyalet yönetimlerinin yetki alanında yer almasına rağmen, Eğitim Bakanları Konferansı, 2024 yılından beri yapay zekanın kullanımına ilişkin tavsiyelerde bulunuyor. Bu tavsiye kararları yasaklama yerine öğrencilerin yapay zekaya eleştirel yaklaşması ve bu konuda becerilerinin geliştirilmesi gerektiğini içeriyor.
Öte yandan yapay zekanın eğitimde önemli bir destek sağlayabileceği de açık. "Yapay zeka konuları ders kitaplarından çok daha iyi anlatıyor" diyen Jakob, bu nedenle birçok temel konuyu yapay zekâdan yardım alarak öğrenmeyi tercih ettiğini söylüyor.
Öğretmen Julian Hinn de bu görüşe katılıyor: "Yapay zeka, öğrencilerin kullandığı dile ve ihtiyaçlarına çok daha iyi uyum sağlayabiliyor. Öğretmenlerin bunu her zaman yapması mümkün olmayabiliyor."
Hinn, bu nedenle de öğrencilerin 10'uncu sınıftan itibaren yapay zeka ile çalışmaya başlamasını önemli buluyor. Üst sınıflarda ise öğrencileri bilinçli olarak yapay zekaya soru sormaya teşvik ediyor. Hinn, "Daha sonra öğrencilerle birlikte verilen yanıtların kalitesini değerlendiriyoruz" diyor.
9'uncu sınıfa kadar ise yapay zekanın daha sınırlı bir şekilde kullanılması gerektiği görüşünde olan Hinn, bunun nedenini "Bu dönemde temel becerilerin henüz gelişme aşamasında olması" olarak açıklıyor.
Franziska Müller de üst sınıflarda yapay zeka uygulamalarını derslerinde daha sık kullanıyor. Ancak bazı aşamalarda öğrencilerin kendi başlarına düşünmelerini sağlamak amacıyla bu araçların kullanımını tamamen yasakladığı da oluyor. Müller, "Yapay zeka kullanmanın ne kadar cazip olduğunu çok iyi anlayabiliyorum" diyor.
Yapay zeka doğru kullanıldığında öğrencilerin başarısını artırabilirken, yanlış şekilde kullanıldığında ise öğrenme sürecini olumsuz etkileyebiliyor. Ancak araştırmaların ortaya koyduğu başka bir sorun daha var: Yapay zekâ, eğitimdeki eşitsizlikleri büyütebilir.
Brookings Institution'ın araştırmasına göre, temel becerileri sağlam olan öğrenciler yapay zeka sayesinde öğrenmelerini daha da geliştirebiliyor ve akranlarına kıyasla daha hızlı ilerleyebiliyor.
Buna karşılık temel bilgi eksiklikleri bulunan öğrenciler, yapay zekanın hatalı yanıtlarını daha kolay kabul ediyor, düşünme sürecini bu araçlara devredebiliyor ve sonuç olarak daha da geride kalabiliyor.
PISA araştırması da daha avantajlı sosyoekonomik koşullara sahip ailelerden gelen çocukların genellikle eğitime daha güçlü bir başlangıç yaptığını ortaya koyuyor. Bu durum, yapay zekanın eğitimdeki fırsat eşitsizliğini daha da artırabileceğine işaret ediyor. Başlangıçta avantajlı olanlar daha hızlı ilerlerken, dezavantajlı konumdakiler geride kalabiliyor.
Yapay zeka yaygınlaşırken öğretmenlere de önemli görevler düşüyor. Öğretmenlerin, öğrencileri düşünmeye teşvik etmeleri ve onlara kendi sorumluluklarını hatırlatmaları gerekiyor.
Okul gazetesi çıkardığını belirten Julian Hinn, "Öğrencilere her zaman şunu söylüyorum: Yapay zeka kullanabilirsiniz, ancak sonunda kendi kaleminizden çıkmış bir yazı yazmış olmanın verdiği duygu bambaşka" diyor.
Hinn de Müller de öğrencilerin bireysel sorumluluğun önemini kavrayabileceği konusunda iyimser. Çünkü aksi durumda bunun sonuçları en geç yazılı sınavlarda ortaya çıkıyor. Bu sınavlarda herhangi bir yardımcı araç kullanılmıyor.
Böylece öğrenciler, konuları gerçekten kendi başlarına anlayıp anlayamadıklarıyla yüzleşmek zorunda kalıyor.

Moms give the best gifts, so it stands to reason that you should get the best gifts for Mom when you're shopping for her in any scenario. That includes Mother's Day , her birthday, Christmas, Hanukkah, or any other holiday in your family's life that includes gift-giving . The holiday season is now upon us, and I've added a few gift ideas with that time of year in mind.
If you're worried you're going to give her a disappointing gift or something she already has, fear not: I've gathered the coolest things we recommend here at WIRED that just about any mom will love. From wellness gadgets that can improve her skin to the best tote bags I've tried, and even a device that puts her digital calendar in an IRL device , moms everywhere can get a ton out of these gifts. Many of these are items I've given to my mother, or other WIRED staffers have given to theirs. Or they might be at the top of my own wish list as a mother of a 4-year-old.
Updated November 2026: I've added Therabody's Theraface Mask Glo, Omnilux's Contour Gloves, WanderFull's HydroBag, and Nuuly's clothing subscription as new gifts to this guide.
The must-have gadget for women of almost any age is an LED mask . These masks promise to use red light to erase wrinkles, brighten your skin, and keep acne at bay. I haven't seen much change in my wrinkles in my year-plus of regularly using a red-light mask, but I can confirm it makes my skin brighter and calms down acne and scars much faster when I'm regularly treating my skin, and I always get compliments on how nice my skin looks when I'm regularly using it. Therabody's TheraFace Mask Glo has a range of treatments with both red and blue light, a unique vibration therapy feature, and removable eye shields if you don't want the light in your eyes.
Look, nothing says mom life like looking for the perfect bag. I'm in a massive tote phase of my life; I somehow need to either lug an armload of items for myself and my son (or just myself!) or I only need a tiny belt bag. There's no in between.
The Yardsale Day Bag has been my go-to for a variety of needs, from a colorful personal item for a flight to a gym bag to the aerial studio. It's got a waterproof bottom that makes me happy to bring it to the zoo's splash pad, and a magnetic middle separator you can flex to separate the middle of the bag into two medium sections to better divide all your items. Plus, there are a handful of side pockets inside, but none are large enough for my massive Owala water bottle. I have the 30L in Butter, but there's also a smaller 20L version if you're looking for something a little more compact.
If your mom wants something a little more stylish, the Alex Mill totes are always on my mind. They come in a variety of gorgeous colors and are made of coated canvas, so they can put up with daily adventures, and you can customize them with your mom's initials (or even just the word “mom”!) with Alex Mill's hand-painted letter service. It's a simpler tote with no other pockets, but you can use the top snaps to let out the sides or tuck them in, depending on how much space Mom needs on a given day. The weathered color and vibe of these bags also feel perfect for the fall season.
My latest favorite family planning gadget is a digital wall calendar . These handy devices take the Google Calendar I live by (and just about any other digital calendar, if your mom isn't a Google girl) and put it on a physical device I can quickly tap into without needing to grab my phone or bark at Alexa . The Skylight Calendar 2 is my favorite, because it not only includes to-do lists, meal planning, and a recipe book but also doubles as a digital photo frame. That means it displays cute photos of my family most of the time, and then, with a simple tap, it opens the calendar or whatever page I was last on to show me what's on my family's schedule. It does have a subscription fee, though, to get the digital photo frame feature and a few other options, like meal planning. But I think it's well worth it to get so many features in a single device. You can also gift her kiddo a Skylight Buddy ($140) so that she doesn't have to remind them to check the main calendar for their chores; it'll appear on their own device if they have a Buddy.
To me, motherhood is all about change. It's most obvious at the start of motherhood, when your body changes a lot over the course of nine months, but motherhood encompasses the rest of our lives, and our bodies and style change a lot over that time. One of the biggest giveaways that time has gone by is our clothes—how well they fit for our current stage, whether they reflect the time of our life right now, and if we're bored out of our skull with everything but don't want to buy an entirely new closet.
I've been loving renting from Nuuly this pregnancy because the brand has an entire maternity section that lets me find pieces to fit me in this short—but very different size—season of my life. My older mother also loves having a clothing subscription because she gets bored of her outfit options to wear into the office, and I loved it for the same reason when I had my first clothing subscription right out of college. If Mom has been talking about wanting some new looks but feels overwhelmed about what she wants to invest in, these rental services are a fun way to get a lot of new clothes in your life without having to store them or spend as much as you would have (some of my favorite maternity clothes I've gotten through Nuuly would have cost me $200 apiece!) The service costs $98 a month, but your first month is discounted to just $60. There's one piece I miss already that might drive me to pick up a second subscription, which would genuinely be cheaper than buying the piece I want brand new.
For years, the go-to gift for a woman in my family, mother or not, was shopping in the jewelry section of a department store. My mom even helped orchestrate this for the rest of the aunties and grandmas, but now, as a mom myself, I find myself interested in jewelry that tells a story about my family and children instead of just any old set. (Except extra earrings for my earring stack, a gift I'm thrilled to get, because there's never enough.)
I love these pieces from Gorjana and BaubleBar that you can customize. Gorjana has a ton of charms you can add to its necklaces or bracelets to reflect Mom’s kids’ initials, birthstones, or anything else; I paired a charm of my son’s first initial ($50) with the Wilshire Adjustable Necklace ($68) . If she's more of a ring gal, BaubleBar's Toi et Moi ring ($78) lets you choose two birthstones to display. I chose my and my son's birthstones, but luckily his sibling-to-be will also have a red birthstone, so it'll remain a perfect reflection of my kids and me for years to come.
This item was literally made for sports moms: a padded stadium cushion with a wearable blanket inside. My son plays on three sports teams, so I do a lot of sitting outside on bleachers and turf sidelines—and often at night, when it’s freezing. I’ve tried many things to keep warm, from heated jackets to HotHands , but nothing has worked as well as this water-resistant blanket, which unfurls to 50 x 70 inches and sports a clip at the front so you can wear it like a cape. It can also be used for picnics or as a spot for younger siblings to sit and read during tournaments. It’s also not hard to fold it back up and fit it inside the seat part (which is 1 inch thick without the blanket inside). It comes in six colors, so you can be sure to find one that matches your giftee’s kid’s team or school colors. —Kat Merck
As a mom, I take a lot of photos of my family. A lot . And sometimes it feels like all those great photos of my son's milestones go to my camera roll and photo storage to die. There are two solutions I love for this that are incredibly giftable: a digital photo frame she can instantly upload images to, and a printed photo book where you can take the best of the best and put them …

Relatives of the missing victims flocked to the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones
A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official says.
Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers show officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims on Sunday, with small fires still burning in some spots.
Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters showed.
The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, located in Cikande in Indonesia’s Banten province about 50km from the capital, caught fire on Saturday afternoon, search and rescue official Rizky Dwianto said on Sunday.
“All elements of the joint SAR [search-and-rescue] team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritising the safety of personnel in the field,” he added.
Rizky said four people were injured and taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic.
Firefighters were alerted about 4.30pm on Saturday and found the building already engulfed in flames when they arrived, fire official Tubagus Machfudz told local broadcaster Kompas TV.
“When we arrived … a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company’s protection system was functioning properly or not,” he said.
The Banten province governor Andra Soni told reporters overnight that an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.
The cause of the incident is still under investigation, the local disaster agency said in an Instagram post on Sunday.
In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.
In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.

Whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land. After many work trips and family vacations I’ve tested several—both universal and basic options—and my favorites will work in most parts of the world.
The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials , Best Travel Tech for Families , Best Travel Pillows , and Best USB-C Cables .
Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.
There’s a ton to like about this 100-watt universal travel adapter from reliable travel brand Ceptics. It covers more than 200 countries and can charge multiple gadgets in a hurry. The classic slider design pushes out EU, UK, and US plugs, and you can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia and China. I love how securely the plugs lock into place; you must press down firmly to slide them back. You have a universal input socket, an additional side socket for US or Japan plugs, and two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports on the bottom. But what makes this travel adapter my favorite is the retractable USB-C cable. It’s around 25 inches long, the end sticks to the adapter magnetically, and it saves you from having to pack an extra cord. The cable can deliver up to 100 watts in total. The USB-C ports support up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports go up to 12 watts.
For all of its strengths, though, it does provide an unfortunate lack of any grounding. Grounding is meant to reduce the risk of an electric shock if there’s a fault, such as a loose wire inside a device with a metal case. ( This video explains grounding well. ) Thankfully, there’s overload protection with a 10-amp fuse, and it also comes with a spare. But you should not use this adapter with any device with a third metal ground pin on its plug.
I also tested the 140-watt Ceptics 6-in-1 model ($51) , which omits the cable but has three USB-C ports and one USB-A, and the excellent 70-watt model ($40) , which has the retractable cable but fewer ports and loses the extra outlet. Both are great alternatives.
Perhaps the smallest travel adapter that's still practical to use, the Epicka Air measures 3.46 x 1.97 inches and is just 1.19 inches thick, with the prongs folded away. It’s easy to pack but still feels reasonably sturdy in use. You get one USB-A and three USB-C ports. The first three ports offer up to 15 watts apiece, and the last USB-C port on the right can go up to 65 watts. But 65 watts is also the maximum output across the four ports, so it gets divided if you plug in multiple devices. But if you use the AC outlet too, and you can charge up to five devices at once.
When I first tested the 40-watt version ($25) , I wasn’t sure about this travel adapter, but after using the 65-watt model for a while, I’ve grown to like it. I still think this style of folding design can be a bit fiddly to use, and the prongs sometimes fold back if you bump them while plugging in. But the placement of the EU prongs in the middle helps it stay plugged in more reliably than some larger sliding cube adapters; the US prongs lock into place, and I didn’t have any issues with the UK prongs.
This budget Ceptics device proves that you don’t need to spend that much money to snag one of the best travel adapters. It covers more than 150 countries, with sliders you push to reveal the three most common international plugs—EU, UK, and US. You can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia or China. The sliders lock into place securely, and there’s a button on the side for retracting them. This plug’s universal outlet can recharge your power-hungry devices, like laptops and camera batteries. Two USB-C and two USB-A ports on the bottom, plus a USB-C port on the side, can handle phones , tablets , smartwatches , and Kindles . Each USB-C port can deliver up to 15 watts, and each USB-A port up to 12 watts. While it's not as fast as some of my picks above, you won't care if you tend to charge your gadgets overnight.
There’s no grounding, so don’t plug devices with a third metal ground pin into this adapter. There is an 8-amp fuse for safety, and it comes with a spare. It is also certified by RoHS and CE.
What I love about this sturdy, compact plug adapter is the lack of sliding pins or moving parts to worry about. It stays put in the outlet. On the downside, it can be tough to use all the outlets simultaneously, as larger plugs, like the MacBook power adapter, tend to block one of the other US outlets. It does not offer surge protection, and the Type G adapter maxes out at 3,250 watts (250 volts, 13 amps), while the EU and other versions top out at 2,500 watts.

Universal adapters don't always work properly everywhere, and most don’t have grounding. The cheaper and more reliable alternative is to buy individual adapters. For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt. The biochemist, who runs a lab at the French National Institute for Agriculture, Food, and Environment, wanted to know how much carbon is released by soil—just dirt alone, completely devoid of life. His team sealed dirt into jars and blasted them with sterilizing gamma radiation. Then they waited for the carbon dioxide released by the soil—a sign of ongoing microbial respiration —to drop.
They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months. Under a microscope, the irradiated soil showed no signs of life, but it continued to emit carbon dioxide. The soil wouldn’t stop breathing.
Fontaine’s lab repeated the experiments and produced the same results. Finally, convinced that they weren’t dealing with an artifact of the experimental setup, they set out to find the source of breath in dead soil.
Now, Fontaine and his colleagues have reported that their soil samples continued to consume oxygen and spew carbon dioxide for six years. In a 2025 paper in Science Advances , they proposed that a metabolic process that powers much of life is also possible outside living cells. Their experiments point to how it could work in dirt, absent the living proteins that would typically organize it. If they’re right, some biochemical reactions, such as those that release the energy of carbon-rich sugar molecules , may not be unique to living things. Such reactions—known as metabolism when performed by cells—could even predate life on Earth, Fontaine said.
The experiments show “what happens to biomolecules when they’re left to their own devices,” said Joseph Moran, an organic chemist at the University of Ottawa who was not involved with the research. They’re finding that the chemistry of life is not exclusive to life , he added. “It’s the chemistry of geology .”
When he made this accidental discovery, Fontaine was trying to establish a baseline for carbon in lifeless soil. Using a sterile syringe, the researchers periodically sampled the air in a hermetically sealed jar containing soil and measured its carbon content using a mass spectrometer. After radiation wiped out the soil microbes , the carbon emission rate declined quickly but didn’t disappear. It remained stable for over 100 days.
When he shared the results with other researchers, they advised him to treat it as an experimental artifact—a source of error not worth ferreting out—and move on. But he couldn’t. He needed to understand whether a metabolic process only known to occur in biological cells—a precisely orchestrated sequence of chemical reactions, requiring several molecules and enzymes—was unfolding in sterile soil. To see what was happening, his team added a dash of enzymes extracted from yeast cultures. Immediately, the soil’s carbon emissions spiked. This, they speculated, was because the enzymes had ramped up a reaction that was already happening.
Convincing the scientific community, however, was an uphill battle. When Fontaine submitted the manuscript to journals for publication, some reviewers “were highly positive, and others were really suspicious, especially concerning the sterility of the soil,” he recalled. In 2013 the results were published in the journal Biogeosciences . Still, Fontaine could not rest. Bruised by the harsh reviews, he decided to definitively prove that his irradiated soil samples remained free of life. Over the following decade, his lab would, in fits and starts, chip away at their obsession.
They considered the possibility that the soil wasn’t really dead and tried to kill it harder with more radiation, pressure, and heat. Still, the soil continued to emit carbon for months.
Through an electron microscope, Benoit Kéraval, then a graduate student in Fontaine’s lab, found cells in the irradiated soil. But staining showed no RNA or DNA molecules, indicating that the cells were definitely dead. When they experimentally added microbes to simulate contamination , the cells rapidly recolonized the soil microcosm and released much more carbon dioxide. So what they were observing in the sterilized sample likely wasn’t a result of inadequate antiseptic measures.
By 2018, when Clémentin Bouquet joined the lab, the team was confident in its findings and ready to dig into the underlying mechanisms.
For six years, Bouquet and Kéraval studied two sets of sealed, irradiated soil samples—one of normal soil and one that was supplemented with glucose. For 142 days, they took regular air samples and saw the daily rate of carbon dioxide emissions decline but not disappear, just as they had before. Then the samples sat in an incubator for over 1,000 days, as the researchers focused on their other experiments into how microbes process and store carbon in soil.
When they measured the samples again, at days 1,606 and 2,442, the emissions had slowed further, but the soil was still breathing. The glucose-augmented samples showed higher emission rates, which strengthened Fontaine’s suspicion that nonbiological catalysts in soil can induce reactions that resemble the metabolic breakdown of sugar.
During metabolism, sugar is broken down into smaller carbon molecules, which feed the Krebs cycle—a series of reactions in which high-energy electrons are stripped from carbon-rich molecules. Electrons liberated by the Krebs cycle then pass through another set of reactions that consume oxygen. For some researchers, it was a stretch to suggest that this process could unfold outside a cell. Fontaine would need to show that soil can play the same role.
He devised a fuel cell that could detect electrons zipping through soil in the form of a current. His team added soil that had been irradiated almost five years earlier and then closed the circuit. A current passed through the soil that was several times higher than in a control setup involving a saltwater solution. According to Fontaine, the experiment demonstrated that sterile soil supports a flow of electrons indicative of processes that resemble the oxygen-dependent metabolism of the Krebs cycle.
It was once thought that the Krebs cycle cannot occur outside the controlled confines of a cell, which teems with enzymes that keep everything ticking along and increases the chances that biomolecules will bump into each other. In a 2025 preprint on biorxiv.org , Fontaine and colleagues reported observing four of the eight intermediate molecules known to be part of the Krebs cycle in 6-month-old sterile soil samples. Many of these molecules formed after the irradiation.
According to the authors, their results suggest that clods of earth can indeed catalyze these reactions without the presence of life.
For Joshua Schimel, a soil ecologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, Fontaine’s findings were not too surprising. “Glucose naturally, in the process of being oxidized, is going to form some of these Krebs-cycle intermediates,” he said. Many soils are rich in iron oxides and aluminum oxides, which can catalyze this conversion, he added.
The idea that metals can catalyze biochemical reactions is central to a theory about the origins of life that has emerged over the last decade. Metals such as iron and zinc sit at the core of many of the most ancient enzymes found across life forms. Some researchers, including Moran, believe they might have catalyzed these reactions before life emerged. Studies, including his , suggest that the chemical reactions that break down and construct glucose derivatives, which are normally associated with life, might have existed before the enzymes and genes that enable them in living cells.
“There’s a handful of researchers like myself that think, actually, we should organize our thoughts about life in a different way—that we actually should put metabolism at the base of what life is doing and then genes are a way of controlling that at a higher level,” Moran said.

GLP-1 drugs could cut food demand enough to free farmland larger than Italy.
GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.
The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.
With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.
The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift toward healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable, and more appealing.
Food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade, and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.
Lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.
It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.
Obesity has often been framed as a “lifestyle disease,” blaming individual people for not having enough willpower . But diets are shaped by what food is available, what it costs, how it’s marketed, where shops are located, and what’s most convenient. In many high-income countries, it is remarkably easy to consume large amounts of cheap, energy-dense food. Society tells people to make healthier choices while surrounding them with an environment that often encourages the opposite.
The UK government-commissioned national food strategy , finalized in 2021, made this point clearly: improving diets can’t simply be about asking individuals to choose better. The wider food environment needs to change to make the better choice the easy one.
Our findings shouldn’t be taken to mean that people living with obesity have a responsibility to lose weight to reduce the environmental impacts of food production. Rather, our research examines the wider consequences that changes in food demand could have across the food system.
A healthier diet is not necessarily just a diet with fewer calories. It could mean more fruit, vegetables, and other nutritious foods, alongside less excessive consumption of foods linked to poor health. These changes affect not only human health but also agriculture, land use, and the environment.
Rather than asking whether GLP-1 medications or healthier diets are the answer, let’s ask how they can work together. Imagine a food system where healthier foods are affordable and accessible, unhealthy options aren’t relentlessly promoted, agricultural policy supports nutritious and sustainable production, and people who need medical treatment can access it. That combination could be far more powerful than any single intervention.
GLP-1 medicines can play an important role in tackling obesity, but they shouldn’t become a technological fix that allows the wider food system to escape scrutiny. They can help people eat less in an unhealthy food environment, but the long-term goal should be to make it easier and more affordable to have a healthier, more sustainable diet.
The remarkable thing about GLP-1 medications may not be that they change how much food people eat. It may be that they show us, with new clarity, just how closely human health, food production, and environmental health are connected, and how much could be gained if we tackled all three together.
Roslyn Henry is Lecturer, School of Biological Sciences, University of Aberdeen and Peter Alexander is Professor of Global Food Systems, University of Edinburgh .

Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents , starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms .
AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf , have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.
Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch , comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.
Some users value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns , pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents.
It’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf.
As the end of the year approaches, multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.
The automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get users in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim , an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life.
Banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major issues, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data shows that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” says Sucharita Kodali , a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases.
“The banks see risks with everything,” she says. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.”
Even though outliers exist, many users are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” says Luca Cian , a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI.
He sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, big-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion.
Cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame ? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens.
Certain credit cards, though, are looking into limited protections for shoppers. Mainly, American Express announced that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can't get your money back from the original retailer.
Banks are pumping out reasonable warnings about third-party agents, but don’t get it twisted. These banks are all-in on first-party tools. “Banks are doing two things at once,” Cian says. “They're locking the door to outside agents and building their own.” Users have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times . Bank of America revamped its new EricaAssist agent this year to help employees. Citigroup even launched an internal development platform specifically centered on agents.
Despite all the hype, Kodali remains skeptical about whether all of this hoopla is even necessary. “The issue with agents and shopping is that, first of all, it is not difficult to buy on Amazon or Walmart or anywhere else,” she says. “In most of those transactions, you don't need an agent.” Agentic shopping often seems to be a solution in search of a problem. Or at least an attempt by AI builders to find a way to earn affiliate revenue, eventually, from their software tools.
Whether AI agents grow in popularity for shopping automation or slowly fade into the digital graveyard, banks are already resolute on the matter. It’s your bot, and your problem.

"I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.
"Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here."
United chief executive Omar Berrada recently spoke about Fernandes' contract situation, saying: "It's true that we're having conversations about his new contract, but I prefer to keep that private."

"We spoke about the contract at the end of last season," Fernandes said.

Emergency workers in Indonesia have recovered at least six body bags after a major factory fire in western Java.
Indonesian police said the blaze broke out at a candy factory in the Serang Regency of Banten province on Saturday.

Reform deputy leader calls Russian leader ‘a murderous dictator’ after US president appears to endorse him
Reform UK and the Conservatives have distanced themselves from Donald Trump after the US president posted a photo of himself shaking hands with Vladimir Putin with the caption: “My friend.”
The US president had already used the term to describe the Russian president while at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, southern China, where he also met the Chinese president, Xi Jinping.
But the photo with Putin, showing Trump leaning towards the Russian leader to talk to him as they met at the summit, posted by Trump on his Truth Social platform overnight, prompted condemnation in the UK.
Asked for his reaction, Richard Tice , the deputy leader of Reform UK, the British party most closely associated with Trump, replied: “Horror.”
He told Sky News: “It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake. He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”
Asked whether Nigel Farage , the Reform UK leader, who is a friend of Trump, would speak to the US president about this, Tice replied: “Oh, there have been a number of occasions where one could agree with Trump, and then disagree with him.
“There have been more occasions recently when clearly we have disagreed with him and said so very explicitly. And in a sense, that’s the nature of long friendships. Sometimes you’ll agree and sometimes you’ll disagree. And, I think the disagreements are growing.”
Reform and the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch, both of whom welcomed Trump’s re-election in 2024, have increasingly tried to dissociate themselves from the US president amid questions over his temperament and judgment, while his attacks on Iran have driven up global energy prices .
Polling last month for YouGov found that just 10% of British people have a favourable opinion of Trump, with 86% holding an unfavourable view. Asked about the “My friend” post, Alex Burghart, Badenoch’s deputy, said he was “very sad” about it.
He told Sky News: “I’m sad and I’m depressed, because the world that I grew up in was one in which the United States was a defender of freedom. I worry that we might be moving into a world where that isn’t the case any more.”
Asked about his party’s previous support for Trump, Burghart replied: “If you look at what the Conservative party is proposing in terms of defence and foreign policy, it’s very clear that we are still on the side of freedom, and we’re the party that has said that we will put up defence spending to what Nato wants it to be.
“So I think you can trust Kemi Badenoch and the Conservatives on this. But, I very much hope that we don’t enter a world in which large, aggressive powers feel that they can occupy their neighbours and get the approval of the United States.”
When asked about the Trump post, Hamish Falconer, a Foreign Office minister, called Putin “a butcher” and said Andy Burnham would make the UK’s views known.
Falconer told Sky News: “The prime minister speaks to the president regularly and is in absolutely no way pulling his punches about the strength of feeling that the UK has as a whole about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.”
